chapter_theme: Sivavakkiyar's attack on ritual and caste at full strength. Temples and tanks are in the mind, Siva is not in brick, black stone or copper, the whispered initiation is a trapper's purse, the Vedas chewed in the mouth are spittle like everything else, there is no mark of caste on flesh, skin or bone, and the impurity people flee from is the blood they were born of. Set against this are the Lord who entered the poet's heart and made it his temple, Vishnu and Siva one as gold under many forms, and the place where mind, life, Sakti and mukti are all absent and Sivayam ripens.
structure_note: The verses run in pairs and triads sharing a device: the counted wasted rites (990), the question-and-answer on temples (998 to 1000), the spittle argument (1004, 1005), the catalogue asked and then negated (1008, 1009), caste (1003, 1010) and menstrual impurity (1012, 1013, continuing into 1014). 1013 and 1014 are joined antadi-fashion, the last words of one opening the next, across the tool's chapter split. 994 and 1001 share a closing line.

989.reading: Lord, beginningless, beginningless before the beginningless: before birth were not woman and man one? On the day the seed of the eyeless man swelled in the womb, how did those of earth and those of heaven come to be?
989.nuance: கண்ணில் ஆணின் சுக்கிலம் is the semen of the man without eyes, which tradition takes as the father who does not see what he begets, or as seed that has no sight of its own; the phrase could also divide as கண்ணில் (in the eye) and be a cipher. The verse asks how gods and humans arise from the same blind seed, and does not answer.

990.reading: How many flowers did I pluck and throw in the past, how many mantras did I recite into the void, how much water did I pour wandering about as a brute, how many times did I come circling Siva's temples?
990.nuance: A first-person confession rather than an address to others: the poet counts his own past flowers, japa, libations and circumambulations and calls them பாழிலே, done into the void. It can be read as mere waste or as a stage he passed through; the verse gives only the count.

991.reading: Jnanis who have known and perceived where the king of the gods dwells: who can know the way they knew it of old? Having no way to tell it other than the meaning of the opened Veda, they do not raise their hands to the god in a built temple.
991.nuance: Line 3 is compressed: விண்ட வேதப் பொருளை அன்றி may mean the jnanis speak only the Veda's inner meaning, or that there is no telling their knowing except as the Veda's meaning. கண்ட கோயில் is the temple one sees, built and visible, as against the dwelling they have found.

992.reading: The lazy say 'far, far, far'; the Supreme is spread everywhere as earth and sky; you mutes who run through town, country and forest searching, know and perceive him straight within yourselves and stand.
992.nuance: சோம்பர் (the lazy) is pointed: those who say the Lord is far are not the strenuous pilgrims but the idle, since the search outside is a way of not looking within. ஊமைகாள் (mutes) is Sivavakkiyar's regular address for those who recite without knowing.

993.reading: As gold is one and the forms differ in their nature, so the red-eyed Mal and Isa shine together within us; you shining people who talk quarrels, the name that stands as everything is this name, this name.
993.nuance: விங்களம் is sectarian wrangling between Vaishnava and Saiva. The gold and its forms is a stock figure for one substance under many shapes; here it is turned on the two gods, and the 'name' at the end is left unnamed, which fits the ராம verses before and 1022 after.

994.reading: Hear the Vedic saying, you who kindle the fire, pour in the ghee and day after day bathe eagerly in water: if you can think of the fire and the water within you and tell of them, can you not follow and join the unshrinking light?
994.nuance: வேதவாக்கியம் கேளுமின் turns the Vedic authority against its own rites: the real Vedic word is that fire and water are within. ஆகுமோ with -ஓ is a rhetorical 'will it not?', shared with 1001.

995.reading: The Supreme who has no song, the lord of the highest world, the lord who has no country, who shares the woman: the mantra muttered about him, drawing the disciple close and covering the mouth, is the trappers' drawstring purse snapping shut without a sound.
995.nuance: The verse mocks the whispered initiation (the ear-mantra). குசுகுசுப்பை is glossed by the editors as a purse that closes with a string, and வேட்டகாரர் as hunters or trappers, so the secret teaching is a snare that shuts on the disciple. The syntax of the last line is loose and the exact object of the mockery, the guru's greed or the secrecy itself, is open.

996.reading: As the tender coconut's water is gathered inside the red coconut, the Lord came, entered my heart and made it his temple; and since the Lord entered my heart and took it as his temple, I do not open my mouth before the people of the world.
996.nuance: The coconut holds its water unseen inside the shell, so the figure is of a presence hidden within. The result is silence toward others, not preaching; compare 982, where knowing ends in a mute body.

997.reading: Fools who, perversely, ring the bell and carry the bees' leavings to pour over a chiselled stone! Even the gods who stand apart look at me and know; was it to end my being split in parts that the gurus set their feet on me?
997.nuance: மணி துலக்கி is ringing or polishing a bell; வண்டின் எச்சில் is honey, called the bee's spittle in advance of the spittle argument at 1004; ஊறுபட்ட கல் is the cut stone of the image. The last two lines are hard: கூறுபட்டுத் தீர்க்கவோ may mean the guru's foot on the poet's head ended his dividedness, or that the poet, unlike the fools, was marked out. The placing of the guru's feet is the Saiva initiation.

998.reading: What is a temple, what are tanks? You slaves who worship temples and tanks! The temple is in the mind and the tanks are in the mind; there is no becoming and no perishing, none at all.
998.nuance: The last line widens the point: what is in the mind neither comes to be nor passes away, unlike built shrines and dug tanks. Tirumular also makes the heart the temple, but keeps the outer temple as a stage; Sivavakkiyar does not.

999.reading: Brick, black stone, the red jati lingam, copper and brass: you say Siva dwells in these. After you have known your own doctrine and known yourselves, will not the Lord who fills the hall become dance and song?
999.nuance: சிவந்த சாதி லிங்கம் is the reddish lingam of a particular stone kind (ஜாதி). உம்மதம் அறிந்து can be 'knowing your own creed' or 'knowing your own self' (உம்மது); the next phrase, உம்மை நீர் அறிந்தபின், makes self-knowledge the hinge. The dance in the hall is the Chidambaram dance made inward.

1000.reading: Fools who do puja crying 'puja, puja': in the self that holds the puja, where was the puja received? Did the one with a beginning receive it, or the beginningless? Which received it? Say exactly.
1000.nuance: ஆதி and அனாதி are the Lord as manifest, with a beginning in form, and as beginningless; the question is who is the receiver of worship if the Lord is without form or place. The verse demands the answer and gives none.

1001.reading: Though you recite the Rig and the four Vedas till the letters wear away, smear on heaps of ash and babble, the Lord is not there; if, melting your heart, you can speak the truth mingled within, can you not follow and join the unshrinking light?
1001.nuance: பிரான் இரான், the Lord is not (there), is blunt: neither recitation nor the ash that Saivas treat as the Lord's own emblem holds him. உருக்கி நெஞ்சை (melting the heart) is the devotional word, placed against the ritual ones.

1002.reading: Water poured and kept in a vessel, when a fierce fire is set under it: did it hide in the vessel, did the fierce fire drink it, did it hide in the earth, did the long sky take it? Removing the maya of the mind, did it hide within the mind?
1002.nuance: The boiled-away water is a figure for what vanishes at death, the life, or for the world when maya is removed; the questions are the ordinary accounts (body, fire, earth, sky) and the last line is the poet's own answer, that it went into the mind. Whether மனத்துள்ளே கரந்ததோ is a question like the others or the answer is a matter of tone.

1003.reading: What is a Paraiyar woman, what is a Brahmin woman? Is there a number marked on flesh, skin or bone? Is the pleasure of the one different, is the pleasure of the other different? Separate the Paraiyar woman and the Brahmin woman within yourselves and see.
1003.nuance: பணத்தி is read by tradition as the Brahmin woman (பார்ப்பனத்தி shortened), though literally it is a woman of money; the argument needs the two ends of the caste order. இலக்கம் இட்டு is a mark or number stamped on the body. The test is bodily, in flesh and in intercourse, not scriptural, and the verse asks for the distinction to be found inside the questioner.

1004.reading: You call the water you drank in your mouth spittle; should not the Veda chewed in your mouth be called spittle too? You who drink water to make the mouth's spittle go, come back and tell me how the spittle went.
1004.nuance: The argument is from the Brahmin's own purity rule: whatever touches the mouth is எச்சில், so recited scripture is defiled by recitation. The last line adds that the rinsing water that removes spittle is itself spittle, so the rule cannot be satisfied.

1005.reading: The recited Veda is spittle, the inner mantras are spittle, the teachings are spittle, the seven worlds are spittle, the seed in the woman is spittle, the moon is spittle and the light is spittle; there is nothing anywhere in which spittle is not, nothing, nothing.
1005.nuance: 1004 pushed to its end: if contact defiles, everything spoken, taught or born is defiled, down to the moon and the light, and purity has no place to stand. மாது இருந்த விந்து makes birth itself the first contamination, which 1012 and 1013 take up.

1006.reading: How was it before birth? How is it after being born and dying into the earth? If you cannot say it precisely, you people without a mark, I will cut off both your ears with the sword of the five letters.
1006.nuance: The threat is rhetorical: ears that cannot hear the answer are cut by the mantra. குறிப்பில்லாத (without mark or aim) plays on குறித்து (precisely): they have no fixed point from which to answer.

1007.reading: If you shoot the hall with an arrow and say 'move', will it move? If you tell the unshaken milk-ocean 'be troubled', will it be troubled? Will darkness come near the yogi who is free of pleasure? The clear Sivayam within the hall of red gold.
1007.nuance: அசங்கென்றால் சங்குமோ is read as அசங்கு (move) with the sandhi dropped; the hall is the Chidambaram hall and, for tradition, the inner hall. இன்பமற்ற யோகி is the yogi without (worldly) pleasure, free of desire, though the words could be taken as 'joyless'. The three images say the same thing: what is settled cannot be shaken from outside.

1008.reading: What is mind, what is thought, what is life, you Siddhas! What is Sakti, what is Sambhu, what is it that is free of caste distinction? What is release, what is the root, what are the root mantras? In the seed without a seed, say which of these is 'mine'.
1008.nuance: The list runs from the inner faculties to Sakti and Siva, release and mantra, and asks their status in the causeless cause (வித்தில்லாத வித்து). The last phrase, இதினெனதென்று, is read as 'which of these is mine' or 'what is this'; the question is answered by negation in 1009, so the two verses are one argument.

1009.reading: The place where one stands without mind, without thought, without life, without Sakti, without Sambhu, without caste distinction, without release, without root and without the root mantras: in the seed that bore this art, Sivayam ripened.
1009.nuance: The same list as 1008 with அற்று (without) after each item; even Sakti, Siva as Sambhu and release are negated, and what remains is named Sivayam, the five letters as the Lord. The editor's heading ஒடுக்க நிலை (the state of involution) fits. விலைந்ததே is read as விளைந்ததே (ripened, came forth); வித்தை (the art, knowledge) may also be வித்தை, 'the seed' as object.

1010.reading: What is caste? Is not all water gathered water? Is not the gate of the elements one, are not the five elements one? Are not ear-ring, bracelet, wire and anklet one gold? What kind of nature is this nature that proclaims caste difference?
1010.nuance: The argument of 993 (one gold, many forms) is turned from the gods to people: all bodies are the same five elements and come through the same gate (பூதவாசல், the womb). சாதி is asked about as a thing, and the answer offered is that it has no substance.

1011.reading: Milked milk does not go back into the udder, churned butter does not go back into the buttermilk; the sound of a broken conch and lives do not go back into the body; the opened flower and the fallen fruit do not go back onto the tree; the dead are not born, no, no, not at all.
1011.nuance: On the plain reading the verse denies rebirth outright, against the Kural, the Tirumanthiram and the whole tradition of births to be cut. Tradition softens it: the dead do not return to this body, or those who have died to the self are not born again. The images all say one thing, that what has left its source does not re-enter it, and the fourfold இல்லை leaves little room for the softer sense.

1012.reading: When it lay in the inner room you did not call it impure; when it knew the bathing place and bathed you did not call it impure; when it knew the drum and you were born you did not call it impure; how then will you come to join the faultless Lord?
1012.nuance: தூமை is menstrual impurity. The 'it' is the blood: in the womb-room it became the child, at the ghat it was washed, at the birth announced by the drum it was you; none of these was called impure, so calling it impure now is incoherent. Line 3's ப்றையறிந்து is corrupt (பறையறிந்து, knowing the drum, or பிறையறிந்து, knowing the crescent, that is the month), and the last line's logic, why the inconsistency bars union, is compressed.

1013.reading: Poor ones who droop and wander saying 'impurity, impurity': while the impure woman is still there, where did the impurity go? You dive like tortoises and recite the many Vedas; the impurity gathered and rolled itself into word-gurus.
1013.nuance: The last line is the sting: the Veda-reciting teachers are themselves the clotted menstrual blood they shun, since that is what every body is made of. ஆமைபோல முழுகி, diving like a tortoise, mocks the repeated ritual immersion. சொற்குருக்கள் (gurus of words) opens 1014, which continues the chain.

links.note: Tirumular tells the devotee to seek through lands, towns and holy temples, sing 'Siva Peruman' and bow, and the Lord will then take the heart as his temple: outer chariyai leads to the inner one. Sivavakkiyar counts his own flowers, japa, libations and circlings of Siva temples and calls them done into the void (பாழிலே). On the reading that 990 dismisses the rites as waste rather than as a stage he outgrew, the two disagree about whether temple service leads anywhere.

Tirumular says the Lord is not in the mansion, hall, courtyard, temple or holy garb but in the hidden place in the heart of those who have given up longing; Sivavakkiyar says the jnanis who have found where the Lord dwells do not raise their hands to the god in a built temple. Both locate him away from the shrine; Tirumular names the condition (longing given up), Sivavakkiyar the result (no hands raised).

967 shows crores running and seeking the light mingled within until they wither and die; 992 names the error, that the lazy call the all-pervading Lord 'far' and run through town, country and forest, and gives the remedy, perceive him straight within and stand.

Both use one gold under many ornaments for the gods: Tirumular says the many gods appear many as ornaments do though they are gold, and makes the Mistress their cause; Sivavakkiyar says Mal and Isa are one gold in differing forms and that sectarian quarrel misses it. The image is the same, the conclusion drawn (Sakti as cause, or sects as error) differs.

Tirumular ranks the ways: those who know only bathing cannot join the Lord, and he is within the minds of those whose knowledge is clear. Sivavakkiyar tells the daily fire-kindlers and bathers that the fire and water are within them and only that knowing joins the light. Both keep the rite's elements and move them inside.

Both turn on the whispered ear-mantra: Tirumular calls the gods who do ear-mantras and lay out the oblation kitchen for their own gain a cruel gathered mantra; Sivavakkiyar calls the mantra muttered with the mouth covered a trappers' purse snapping shut. Tirumular's target is self-interest in the rite, Sivavakkiyar's the secrecy itself.

Both poets report the same event in the first person: Tirumular brought the bright reality in and made his heart its temple on earth, and swears it is truth, not falsehood; Sivavakkiyar says the Lord entered his heart and made it his temple, hidden like water in a coconut. Sivavakkiyar adds the consequence, that he no longer opens his mouth before the world.

Tirumular makes the heart the great temple, the body the shrine, the mouth the tower gate and the soul the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar says temple and tanks are in the mind. Tirumular builds the inner temple as a full correspondence to the outer one; Sivavakkiyar asks what the outer one is at all.

Tirumular says that for those clear through and through the soul is the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar denies that Siva dwells in brick, black stone, the red lingam, copper or brass and says that self-knowledge is what makes the Lord's dance appear. Both move the linga from stone to the self.

The two verses share their last line, சுருக்கம் அற்ற சோதியைத் தொடர்ந்து கூடல் ஆகுமோ, and the same shape: an outer practice (fire and bathing in 994, Vedas and ash in 1001) set against an inner act (knowing fire and water within, speaking the truth with a melted heart) that alone reaches the light.

The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the Paraiyar woman and the Brahmin woman differ in flesh, skin, bone or pleasure. The Kural still allows distinction by deed; Sivavakkiyar's bodily test allows none.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them and that austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Sivavakkiyar says there is no mark of caste on flesh, skin or bone. The Naladiyar replaces caste with merit; Sivavakkiyar removes it and puts nothing in its place.

Tirumular says there is no need of purification for one who stands free of pollution (துடக்கு); Sivavakkiyar says Veda, mantra, worlds, seed, moon and light are all spittle, so purity has no ground anywhere. Tirumular sets purity aside for one who has passed beyond it; Sivavakkiyar denies it was ever coherent.

1008 asks what mind, thought, life, Sakti, Sambhu, release, root and root mantras are in the seedless seed; 1009 repeats the list with அற்று after each and names what stands where all of them are absent as Sivayam ripened in the seed. The question is answered by negating every term it asked about.

993 says gold is one and the forms differ, and applies it to Vishnu and Siva; 1010 says ear-ring, bracelet, wire and anklet are one gold, and applies it to castes, with the five elements and the one womb-gate as the shared substance. The same figure does the work against sect and against caste.

Tirumular says that for those who set Nandi firmly in love there is no impurity, no pride, no caste and no qualities to take on; Sivavakkiyar asks what caste is when all bodies are the same water, the same five elements and the same gold. For Tirumular caste falls away at a stage of knowledge; for Sivavakkiyar it never had a nature.

The Kural says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking after sleep, a cycle that resumes; Sivavakkiyar says the dead are not born, as milk does not return to the udder or the fallen fruit to the tree, and denies it four times. On the plain reading of 1011 the two make incompatible claims about what follows death; on tradition's softer reading (not born into this body again) the conflict dissolves.

Tirumular's Siddhanta premise is that the soul is reborn until it rests in the Lord and birth is cut off (பிறப்பறுந்தானே); cutting birth is an attainment. Sivavakkiyar's plain statement that the dead are not born again makes rebirth not a bond to be cut but a thing that does not happen. The tension holds on the plain reading of இறந்தவர் பிறப்பதில்லை.

1013 ends with the impurity rolled into word-gurus (சொற்குருக்கள் ஆனதே) and 1014 opens with the same words, then extends the list: light-bodied gurus, true gurus, sat-gurus, gurus of deeds, puja and sastra are all the same clotted blood. The antadi chain crosses the tool's chapter boundary.

source_issues: 1012 line 3 reads ப்றையறிந்து with a stray pulli on the first letter; the word is corrupt, probably பறையறிந்து or பிறையறிந்து.
1009 has விலைந்ததே for விளைந்ததே and மூத்தியற்று for முத்தியற்று, both apparently copying slips.
1005 is punctuated with '.,' after each half-line, an editor's marks rather than the text.
1013 and 1014 are joined antadi-fashion (the last words of 1013 open 1014) across the tool's split between chapters 56 and 57.
